1.title: Choose crops, space and a first customer
1.intro: Vertical gardens grow food or plants in stacked layers indoors or on walls. They suit places with little land and high prices for fresh produce.
pts: Compare crops by days to harvest, price per kilogram and light needed: leafy greens and herbs turn fastest; fruit crops need more space and light.
Find a first customer within an hour's drive: restaurants, grocers, food programmes, office tenants who want green walls.
Ask each for weekly volume, price they pay now and the freshness gap you can close.
Write the offer: 'fresh [crop], harvested the day before, delivered twice a week at [price] per kilogram'.
Build a crop table with one row per crop: days to harvest, kilograms per tray, price per kilogram, and revenue per tray (kilograms x price).
Measure your space: write length, width, ceiling height, floor load and where the power and water points are, before you choose a rack layout.
Pick one crop to start. Write why it beats the second choice on speed, price and the risk of loss.
1.ex: Basil sells at 28 per kilogram to restaurants who now pay 36 for imported, so each kitchen saves 8 per kilogram. Demand is 12 kg per week across three kitchens: 12 x 28 = 336 a week in sales, and the buyers save 12 x 8 = 96 a week. This is a small start, which is right for a first customer test.
1.act: Interview five buyers and fill a crop table with price, volume and delivery frequency.
1.std: Five buyers recorded; one crop chosen with reasons.

2.title: Know the rules for growing and selling in Canada
2.intro: Growing under lights is farming, manufacturing and a building project at once.
pts: Food grown for sale must follow food-safety and labelling rules, and which federal, provincial or local rules apply depends on where you sell and what you grow, so check the provincial rule; the local public health unit may inspect washing and packing areas.
Building and fire rules apply to racks, wiring and water; get electrical work done by licensed trades and inspected.
Water use, nutrient discharge and waste are regulated by the municipality and province.
Insurance for crop loss, equipment and liability should be arranged before the first harvest.
Zoning decides whether you may grow and sell food from a warehouse or shop unit. Ask the municipality in writing and keep the reply.
A lease should allow the changes you need, such as extra power and drains. Read it for who pays for repairs and what happens at renewal.
Check the provincial rule for any licence or registration needed to sell food directly to restaurants or shops.
2.ex: Row: 'Pack leafy greens for sale | federal or provincial food inspection office and local health unit | register and follow wash and pack rules | before first sale | inspection report'. A table of 10 rows with 3 rows needing a permit means 3 of 10 (30%) have a waiting time to plan around, so list those first.
2.act: Build the rules table for a rented warehouse unit in your province.
2.std: Each row cites an official source and date.

3.title: Design the system and grow a first crop
3.intro: Good vertical growing is a controlled loop: light, water, nutrients, air and time.
pts: Choose a system: hydroponic (roots in water), aeroponic (roots misted) or a soil-based wall, and write why it suits your crop and budget.
Set written targets for light hours per day, nutrient strength (conductivity), water pH, temperature and humidity.
Log these readings daily and change only one setting at a time so you can see what caused any change.
Track yield per tray and days to harvest for every cycle so that you can compare runs.
Calibrate the pH and conductivity meters before the first crop with the test liquids the maker supplies, and write the date.
Test the water you use. Hard or chlorinated water changes nutrient needs, so record what the local supply report or your own test shows.
Keep a seed lot number for each tray, and compare yield between lots.
3.ex: Lettuce: 28 days to harvest, 0.45 kg per tray, 12 trays per rack, 10 racks. One rack gives 0.45 x 12 = 5.4 kg and ten racks give 54 kg per cycle. If one rack fails, the cycle gives 48.6 kg, a loss of 10%.
3.act: Grow one tray cycle; log daily readings and final yield.
3.std: Daily log complete; yield per tray calculated.

4.title: Cost it: power, labour and trays
4.intro: Electricity for lights is usually the largest cost after rent.
pts: Power cost per cycle = lamp kilowatts x hours per day x days x price per kWh.
Add labour for seeding, moving, harvesting and cleaning, using the hours you actually record.
Compute cost per tray and per kilogram and compare them with the selling price.
Test a 10% rise in power price and a 15% yield drop, and show the new margin and break-even for each.
Use your own electricity bill for the price per kWh, with the delivery and rate-class charges included. Check the provincial rate rules for farms or businesses.
Add fixed costs each month: rent, insurance, water, software and a share of your own pay.
Break-even trays per month = fixed cost divided by margin per tray, rounded up.
4.ex: Power per tray: 0.2 kW x 16 h x 28 days = 89.6 kWh; at 0.16 per kWh that is about 14. Add seeds and nutrients 6, packaging 4, labour 14 for 38 variable; price 95 per tray-equivalent gives margin 57 (60%). Break-even is 21,700 / 57 = about 381 trays a month. Power test: a 10% rise in power price adds about 1.4, so variable cost is 39.4, margin 55.6 and break-even is 21,700 / 55.6 = about 390 trays. Yield test: a 15% yield drop cuts revenue to 80.75 and margin to 42.75, so break-even rises to about 508 trays. Teaching figures in CAD.
4.act: Build the cost sheet for your system and compute break-even.

5.title: Run clean, steady operations
5.intro: Hygiene, schedules and records keep crops safe and predictable.
pts: Clean trays and tanks between cycles, sanitise tools and require hand washing at the entry.
Stagger seeding weekly so that harvests arrive steadily.
Scout for pests and mould twice a week and remove problem trays at once.
Keep a harvest and delivery log with batch numbers so that every bag can be traced.
Write a daily checklist by the door: lights on, pumps running, water level, alarms tested, doors closed.
Keep tools and cleaning supplies separate for growing and packing areas.
Train every helper in the hand-washing and illness rules before they touch a crop, and record the date.
5.ex: Batch code 'B-0417-T3' links a delivered bag to the tray, seed lot and cleaning record. If a 28-day crop is seeded weekly across 4 groups of trays, one group is harvested each week, so a customer receives 4 deliveries in a 28-day period.
5.act: Keep a 4-week operations log with batch numbers.
5.std: Every delivery traces back to a tray.

6.title: Sell, deliver and keep the customer
6.intro: Restaurants and grocers value a steady supply and a person who answers.
pts: Offer a standing weekly order with a trial week.
Deliver on a fixed day and time; confirm by message the day before.
Tell the story: seed to harvest dates, no spray, local. Say 'no spray' only if it is true and recorded.
Ask for feedback after four weeks and adjust crop mix.
Price by weight, and show what the buyer saves compared with what they pay now, in dollars per week.
Agree what happens when a delivery is late or short: a credit or a replacement on the next day.
Keep a customer sheet: contact, order, delivery day, price, complaints and next review date.
6.ex: Funnel: 15 visits, 6 samples, 3 trial orders, 2 standing orders. Rates: samples 6/15 = 40%, trials 3/6 = 50%, standing 2/3 = 67%. Overall 2/15 = 13% of visits became standing orders, so 10 more visits would bring about 1 or 2 more.
6.act: Visit ten buyers with samples and record outcomes.

7.title: Manage food safety and power risks
7.intro: A power cut or contamination can end a crop in hours.
pts: List the main risks: power failure, pump failure, contamination, pests and the loss of a buyer.
Set controls for each risk, such as backup power for pumps, alarms, spare parts and regular water tests.
Write a recall plan that shows which batches went to which buyers and how you will tell them.
Write an energy plan: efficient lamps, off-peak operating hours, and renewable power by contract or on the roof where allowed.
Score each risk as chance (1 to 5) times harm (1 to 5) and handle the highest scores first.
Plan for a hot summer or cold winter day: how the room keeps its temperature if cooling or heating fails.
Run a test once a month: switch off the main power and check the alarm and the backup. Write the result.
7.ex: Risk: 'Pump fails overnight | 2 x 5 = 10 | float alarm and spare pump | owner | monthly test'. A contamination risk scored 3 x 5 = 15 ranks higher, so its controls come first.
7.std: Each row has owner and test date.

8.title: Pilot one room and plan growth
8.intro: Prove one room before you build ten.
pts: Run the pilot for 60 days and measure yield, cost per kilogram and orders kept.
Set a stop rule: if yield is below 60% of plan after two cycles, pause and fix the cause.
Scale in steps: open a second room only after the margin holds.
Plan funding from grants for local food and clean technology and from customer pre-orders, but do not count on either until it is confirmed.
Write the plan numbers before the pilot: planned yield per cycle, planned cost per kilogram and planned margin.
Hold a review at day 30 and day 60. Record what changed and why.
Check the funding programmes' rules and dates yourself; do not assume a grant will arrive.
8.ex: Result at day 60: 48 kg per cycle against 54 plan (48/54 = 89%), above the 60% stop line, so proceed. If the yield had been 30 kg (56%), the stop rule would pause the pilot to fix the cause.
8.act: Run the pilot and present review.

quiz: Why compare crops by days to harvest?
Faster crops return cash sooner and fit stacked systems best.
What is usually the largest cost after rent?
Electricity for lights.
How do you compute power cost per cycle?
Lamp kilowatts x hours per day x days x price per kWh.
Why use batch codes?
They trace a delivered bag back to its tray and enable recalls.
Name three growing systems.
Hydroponic, aeroponic and soil-based wall.
What should a risk register include for pumps?
A control such as an alarm and a spare, an owner and a test date.
What is a stop rule in the pilot?
A pre-agreed trigger, such as yield under 60% of plan, to pause and fix.
Why stagger seeding?
Harvests stay steady week to week.
Who inspects wash and pack areas?
Depending on the province, the local public health unit or a provincial inspector may; check the provincial rule.
Why test a 15% yield drop?
It shows whether the business still breaks even under stress.
